name: Asylum / Refugee Status

requirements.blocker_text: Under Law No. 021/2002 (16 October 2002) and its implementing Decree No. 03/014 (5 August 2003), the National Refugee Commission (Commission Nationale pour les Refugies, CNR) -- a public service under the Ministry of Interior, Security, Decentralization and Customary Affairs -- determines refugee status through its Eligibility Commission, with a separate Appeals Commission for challenges. DRC is party to both the 1951 Geneva Convention and the 1969 OAU Convention governing refugees in Africa, and the law requires the CNR to meet applicants' elementary needs (housing, food, health, education) and cooperate closely with UNHCR under Geneva Convention Article 35.
requirements.fix_path: Register with the CNR's Eligibility Commission; appeal to the Appeals Commission if initially refused.

sources.title: Commission Nationale pour les Refugies (CNR), Democratic Republic of the Congo -- official government body page: its status under the Ministry of Interior, its legal basis (Law 021/2002, Decree 03/014), and its Eligibility/Appeals Commission structure

notes: NEW COUNTRY BUILD (Democratic Republic of the Congo). STATUS: PUBLISHED -- direct government sourcing (cnr.cd, DRC's own refugee commission, tier 1), corroborated by UNHCR's hosted primary legal text. GENUINELY FUNCTIONING SYSTEM, ONE OF THE STRONGER FINDINGS IN THIS DATASET: real law (2002), a dedicated standing commission operational since 2004, a named appeals mechanism, and party status to BOTH the 1951 Convention and the 1969 OAU Convention (the latter broadens the refugee definition specifically for African displacement contexts, beyond individualized persecution). This stands in sharp contrast to Uzbekistan, Kuwait, Lebanon, and Syria's absent-or-thin frameworks built earlier in this dataset. CONTEXT WORTH NAMING: DRC is simultaneously one of the world's largest REFUGEE-HOSTING countries (a UNHCR portal reviewed in this build cites over 300,000 Burundian refugees alone, plus populations from the Central African Republic and South Sudan) and one of the world's largest INTERNALLY DISPLACED populations (millions of IDPs from its own eastern-conflict zones) -- this route models only the inbound-hosting side; internal displacement is a distinct legal and humanitarian category not modeled by this dataset's schema, which is oriented around cross-border immigration routes. Exact application-process timelines were not specified in either source -- disclosed as unconfirmed rather than invented. work_rights set 'restricted' (not found detailed as fully open) and family_can_work left null since neither source addressed dependents' work rights specifically.
